strengths: Clear problem motivation and well-articulated solution addressing practical issues in LLM fine-tuning (20-40% noisy preference pairs)
Significant computational efficiency improvement: ~1.5% overhead vs. 10% for RHO-Loss and 4% for one-shot learning, with no reference model training required

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple training paradigms (SFT, DPO, SimPO), model families/scales (LLaMA/Qwen 3B-8B), datasets (Alpaca, Yahoo, UltraFeedback, SHP-2, GSM8K), and parameter-updating approaches (full fine-tuning and LoRA)
Consistent improvements across all settings, with win rates >50% against standard training (60-85% in many cases) and comparable/superior performance to RHO-Loss
Thorough analysis including ablation studies, score distribution visualization, weight dynamics, variability analysis (Tables 4-5), and high/low-scoring examples providing interpretability
Strong reproducibility: detailed algorithms, implementation details, promised code release, and example prompts
Honest discussion of limitations, particularly concerning on-policy methods and holdout set requirements
weaknesses: Core approximation in Equation 6 (ℓ(y | x; θ*(Dt ∪ Dho)) ≈ ℓ(y | x, Dho; θt)) lacks rigorous theoretical justification and formal error analysis; citation of Dai et al. (2023) on ICL-as-gradient-descent applies to few-shot task learning, not approximating parameter update effects

Concerning results in Section C.5: when holdout set is excluded from training, win rates drop significantly vs. RHO-Loss (47.29% vs. 54.03%), suggesting the method may rely on having holdout examples in the training set itself, limiting practical applicability
Limited novelty as primarily an incremental improvement over RHO-Loss (Mindermann et al., 2022), replacing reference model with in-context learning rather than introducing fundamentally new concepts

Significant applicability limitation: method only works for off-policy training (SFT, DPO, SimPO) and cannot handle on-policy RL methods like PPO, which are increasingly important for modern alignment

Evaluation methodology concerns: most experiments use single training runs (though Tables 4-5 provide limited variability analysis); win rates depend on GPT-4o judging which can be noisy; absolute metrics (PPL, BERTScore) show modest improvements in some cases

Design choices insufficiently justified: unclear why k=3 (top-k holdout examples) is universally optimal when k=1, 5, 10 all underperform; sensitivity to embedding model not thoroughly explored despite BAAI/bge-m3 showing improvements; max-min vs. softmax normalization choice minimally justified
Within-batch reweighting normalization (Eq. 8) may miss between-batch dynamics and long-range dependencies; no exploration of global normalization schemes
Limited statistical rigor: most tables lack confidence intervals; only Table 4 provides standard deviations from multiple evaluations; no formal hypothesis testing
